newsitem.title: CANADA: Quebec uncertainty still threatens Canada economy.
newsitem.headline: Quebec uncertainty still threatens Canada economy.

text.p: Despite projections of an across-the-board recovery, Canada's economy will not be able to escape a severe downdraft if Quebec decides to travel the independence route again, economists polled in a Reuters survey say.
Twenty-three out of the 24 economists surveyed in Canada and the United States were optimistic when asked to project Canada's economic future during the next eight quarters.
A healthy dollar, strong growth in gross domestic product (GDP) and a continued merchandise trade surplus are a few of the rewards awaiting Canadians in coming years, they say.
But all bets are off, say the economists, if Canada enters another period of divisive infighting.

The markets will only start pricing in risk once they know a referendum is imminent, said Mark Mullins, chief economist with brokerage firm Midland Walwyn. "Right now, we're taking the premier of Quebec at his word that he will serve out his mandate without another referendum."

Lucien Bouchard, the newly minted premier of Quebec and the most charismatic politician in the predominantly French-speaking province, has pledged not to call another independence referendum before the next provincial election.
Bouchard instead has vowed to concentrate on rebuilding Quebec's debt-laden economy. But the premier has not backed off the idea of eventually holding another referendum on sovereignty.
The separatists, who lost a referendum last October by a thin margin, are determined to reverse that verdict and assert the French-speaking province's right to autonomy.
A year ago, economists warned of a financial meltdown if Quebec voted to break away. Now nobody relishes another tangle with the economics of national division.

Mullins cautioned that his projections of a gradual strengthening of the Canadian dollar -- a projection backed up by 17 of 19 economists polled -- would be blown apart by the onset of another referendum. Mullins is the most bullish economist on the Canadian dollar, projecting it will rise to C$1.2650 (79.05 cents) by the third quarter of 1998.

"I can see it (the Canadian dollar) getting rattled more because most investors came into the last referendum thinking it was going to be a cakewalk," Mullins said. "I think we'll have a really dramatic response next time around."

During the last referendum campaign, the Canadian dollar plunged to C$1.3730 (72.83 cents) on news that the separatist side was leading with just days to go before the vote. The dollar currently is stable around C$1.3500 (74 cents).
John Anania, an economist at the Royal Bank of Canada, agreed that future political instability relating to Quebec could wreak havoc on the dollar and short-term interest rates.
"As the referendum approaches, you would see weakness in the dollar and a narrowing of the spreads in short-term interest rates," he said.
But Anania cautioned that the impact could be offset by the underlying fundamentals of the Canadian economy, which are generally bright.
